title: Development of a Cyber-Physical System for Real-Time Production Monitoring in a Digital Factory
items.abstract:
<jats:p><p><span>This study focuses on the development of a cyber-physical system (CPS) for real-time monitoring and predictive fault detection in a digital factory. By leveraging sensor data from turbines, compressors, and pumps, the system addresses limitations of traditional reactive maintenance approaches. A dataset from Kaggle was utilized, containing sensor readings for temperature, pressure, vibration, and humidity, along with metadata such as equipment type, location, and fault status. The methodology involved data preprocessing, exploratory data analysis (EDA), feature engineering, and predictive modeling using machine learning algorithms.</span></p>
<p><span>Results indicated that vibration and temperature were the most influential predictors of faults, with strong correlation coefficients of +0.79 and +0.67, respectively. Among the tested models, the random forest model achieved the highest accuracy (95%) and F1-score (0.93). The developed CPS features a real-time alert mechanism and an interactive dashboard for monitoring sensor data and fault predictions. While the findings highlight the potential of predictive maintenance to reduce downtime and enhance operational efficiency, future validation in real-world industrial environments is recommended.</span></p></jats:p>

title: Building Trust in Agentic AI: TRACE Framework for Policy-Driven Multi-Agent System Design
container-title: International Journal of Current Science Research and Review
items.abstract: <jats:p>The rapid adoption of multi-agent AI systems— ranging from prescriptive, workflow-driven deployments to fully agentic, autonomous ecosystems—raises urgent challenges for trust, accountability, and regulatory compliance. This paper introduces the TRACE Framework (Trust, Review, Accountability, Critique, Explainability), a governance-first architecture designed to make multi-agent AI systems auditable, policy-aligned, and operationally reliable across varying degrees of agent autonomy. TRACE embeds governance anchors at the agent level, enforces data privacy and policy checks, supplies a dedicated Critic agent for meta-validation, and preserves human-in- the-loop oversight where required. We present a layered architecture that separates Governance & Compliance, Operational Agents, and Oversight & Assurance, and provide a concrete methodology for instrumenting agent behaviour with provenance, explainability outputs, and per-agent metrics. A formal scoring rubric—comprising agent operational metrics, critic checks, and aggregation rules—yields an Overall System Confidence (OSC) that drives automated actions, human escalation, and continuous learning. Finally, we propose a suite of operational KPIs for each layer as Governance and Compliance Indicators (GCI), Agentic Performance Metrics (APM), and Assurance Indicators (AI) that enable financial institutions and other regulated organisations to deploy multi-agent systems that are efficient, auditable, and compliant. TRACE bridges the gap between regulatory expectations and system engineering practice— providing a practical roadmap for trustworthy multi-agent AI deployment in high-stakes domains.</jats:p>

title: AI-Enabled Software and System Architecture Frameworks: Focusing on Smart Cyber-Physical Systems (CPSs)

affiliation.name: University of Colorado Colorado Springs
University of Reading Department of Computer Science
Technische Universitat Munchen
Universiteit Antwerpen

items.abstract:
<jats:p>Several architecture frameworks for software, systems, and enterprises
have been proposed in the literature. They identified various
stakeholders and defined architecture viewpoints and views to frame and
address stakeholder concerns. However, the stakeholders with data
science and Machine Learning (ML) related concerns, such as data
scientists and data engineers, are yet to be included in existing
architecture frameworks. Therefore, they failed to address the
architecture viewpoints and views responsive to the concerns of the data
science community. In this paper, we address this gap by establishing
the architecture frameworks adapted to meet the requirements of modern
applications and organizations where ML artifacts are both prevalent and
crucial. In particular, we focus on ML-enabled Cyber-Physical Systems
(CPSs) and propose two sets of merit criteria for their efficient
development and performance assessment, namely the criteria for
evaluating and benchmarking ML-enabled CPSs and the criteria for
evaluation and benchmarking of the tools intended to support users
through the modeling and development pipeline. This study deploys
multiple empirical and qualitative research methods based on literature
review and survey instruments, including expert interviews and an online
questionnaire. We collect, analyze, and integrate the opinions of 77
experts from over 25 organizations in 10 countries to devise and
validate the proposed framework.</jats:p>

title: Agentic Lab: An Agentic-physical AI system for cell and organoid experimentation and manufacturing
items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                <jats:p>Reproducibility in biological research and manufacturing remains constrained by the complexity of multi-step protocols, fragmented data-analysis pipelines, and the intrinsic variability of experimental execution. Here, we present Agentic Lab, an agentic-physical AI platform that unifies large language model and vision language model (LLMs/VLMs)-driven reasoning with real-world laboratory operations. Agentic Lab uses multi-agent orchestration architecture, comprising of specialized subagents for knowledge retrieval, protocol design, multimodal data analysis, and training-free segmentation and representation learning for intrinsically explainable single-cell and organoid phenotyping. These agents operate under the orchestration of a virtual principal investigator MolAgent that is linked to an augmented reality (AR)-based physical AI interface, which can bridge digital reasoning with human physical execution. Agentic Lab perceives real-world experimental activities, provides context-aware instructions, identifying procedural errors in real time for humans to correct, and continuously evolves with its long-term memory database expanding through the accumulation of experimental data logs from human scientists. This interaction allows scientists and AI agents to collaborate and co-evolve dynamically, closing the loop between planning, action, and analysis in the traditional cell and organoid research lifecycle. We demonstrate Agentic Lab in organoid differentiation from human pluripotent stem cells, where it autonomously generates protocols, monitors culture procedures, and identifies subtle morphological heterogeneity linked to growth conditions. The system interprets these phenotypes, grounds them in literature, and proposes targeted instructions for improving differentiation efficiency. By combining multi-agent reasoning with physical laboratory awareness, Agentic Lab transforms experimentation and biomanufacturing from a static workflow into an adaptive, feedback-driven, bidirectional process that integrates agentic AI into the research lifecycle. This framework establishes a foundation for intelligent laboratories that integrate design, execution, and interpretation within a unified agentic-physical system.</jats:p>

title: Design and Implementation of Agentic AI Pipelines for Enterprise Decision-Making Architecture Patterns for Production Systems
container-title: International Journal of Innovative Research in Engineering & Multidisciplinary Physical Sciences
items.abstract: <jats:p>The emergence of large language models (LLMs) has enabled a new paradigm of autonomous AI agents capable of reasoning, planning, and executing complex multi-step tasks. However, deploying these agents in enterprise environments presents significant architectural challenges around orchestration, tool integration, memory management, and execution reliability. This paper presents Nexus, a reference architecture and implementation for production-grade agentic AI pipelines in enterprise decision-making systems. We formalize reliability semantics (at-most-once, at-least-once, exactly-once) for LLM tool execution, introduce an adaptive reasoning strategy selector that dynamically chooses between Direct, ReAct, and Plan-and-Execute based on task complexity, and present a hierarchical memory system with explicit operational semantics. Evaluation across 500 real enterprise tasks demonstrates 87.6% end-to-end task completion rates with median latency of 1.2 seconds, achieving statistically significant improvements over fixed-strategy baselines (p < 0.01). Ablation studies validate the contribution of individual components. We analyze failure modes, discuss lessons learned from production deployments, and provide guidelines for practitioners building reliable agent systems.</jats:p>

title: <p>Runtime Legitimacy in Autonomous AI Systems:&nbsp;<span>A Cyber Law Framework for Dynamic Authority Management and Decay in Agentic AI</span></p>
items.abstract: <jats:p>The rapid emergence of Agentic AI systems-capable of independent planning, multi-step decision-making, and autonomous execution without direct human intervention-renders the traditional model of static authority delegation inadequate for legal and accountability purposes. This paper proposes a novel framework termed Runtime Legitimacy, coupled with Authority Decay, under which the validity of delegated authority must be re-verified not only at the time of initial grant but continuously, in real time, at the moment of executing any high-risk operation. By shifting the burden of proof from "authority was granted" to "authority remained valid at the moment of execution," this approach transforms continuous monitoring from a technical recommendation into an evidentiary legal obligation. It mitigates unbounded vicarious liability for organizations in the absence of legal personality for the AI system itself and aligns with emerging regulatory requirements, including the EU AI Act's emphasis on continuous oversight, dynamic human-in-the-loop mechanisms, post-market monitoring, and accountability. The framework incorporates risk-based classification of operations, mandatory re-attestation before sensitive actions, escalation to human decision-makers when re-attestation fails, and immutable audit trails for judicial defensibility. An illustrative financial system example demonstrates practical application. While offering significant reductions in civil, criminal, and regulatory liability risks, implementation challenges-such as latency in critical operations and balanced user experience-are acknowledged. This cyber law-oriented model bridges technical architecture and legal imperatives, providing a foundation for governance standards in the era of autonomous AI. The framework is positioned to inform both organizational risk management practices and potential regulatory reform initiatives addressing the unique challenges posed by agentic artificial intelligence systems.</jats:p>

items.abstract: <jats:p xml:lang="en">The Internet is shifting from a human-centric web towards an agentic frontier, with artificial intelligence (AI) agents increasingly integrated into daily life. The transition from instruction-based bots to goal-orientated agents is accelerating, signalling a move from automation to autonomy. According to internal Akamai data, AI bot traffic grew by 300 per cent over the past year, bringing a new kind of Internet traffic characterised by distinct behaviours. As AI agents evolve, existing security defences are proving inadequate; signature-based rules cannot effectively counter reasoning-driven agents. This paper examines the taxonomy of attacks, both AI as a threat and threats targeting AI systems. Whether dealing with aggressive AI inference crawlers such as Bytespider or innovative AI-engineered threats, current security limitations heighten business risks and operational challenges. This necessitates a fundamental evolution, not only of traditional firewalls but also of the security architecture, towards a new, agent-aware defence framework that moves beyond identifying who is accessing resources to understanding the intent and logic of autonomous actors. Semantic firewalls are essential, protecting users and agents at input and output stages while keeping models safe. To enable verifiable autonomy, strategic shifts at the board level are critical, establishing governance frameworks that allow organisations to transition from black-box models to transparent, verifiable glass-box models, paving the way for trustworthy autonomous systems. This article is also included in The Business & Management Collection which can be accessed at https://hstalks.com/business/.</jats:p>

title: Agentic Agriculture: A Comprehensive Survey of AI Agents and Agentic AI in Precision Agriculture
items.abstract: <jats:p>This survey presents a first comprehensive analysis of the emerging paradigm of Agentic Agriculture, tracing the evolution from model-centric artificial intelligence to integrated, goal-driven agentic systems in precision agriculture. It begins with clearly defined research objectives and a structured literature synthesis methodology. The review covers foundational AI agents for core tasks, including sensing and monitoring, decision-support and advisory systems, and robotic field operations such as harvesting, spraying, and crop monitoring. Building on these, the survey examines multi-agent systems enabling distributed farm intelligence through IoT-agent architectures, swarm robotics, and multi-agent reinforcement learning for coordinated farm management and operational optimization. It then advances to Agentic AI, where autonomous agents extend these systems by integrating perception, reasoning, planning, and action into unified workflows. Applications include adaptive irrigation, crop monitoring, and resource allocation, supported by digital twins that evolve from static simulations to closed-loop, decision-driven optimization platforms. The survey further explores autonomous agricultural ecosystems with human-AI collaboration and coordinated robotics, including reinforcement learning-based irrigation and multi-robot harvesting. Finally, it identifies challenges in reliability, safety, data governance, ethics, and regulation. Overall, Agentic AI enables scalable, adaptive, and knowledge-driven agricultural systems, requiring robust integration of data-driven and process-based models for trustworthy deployment.</jats:p>

items.abstract: <jats:p>Aquaponics is a sustainable fish and plant production process in an indoor ecosystem. Recent development in aquaponics has led to the development of new automated technologies which can serve in high automation, efficiency, and waste minimization. Zero-defect production systems are key to high quality in a production environment where cyber-physical systems, data acquisition, and decision-making are paramount. This paper presents a novel framework based on a cyber-physical systems (CPS) architecture that provides data acquisition, data analytics, and data storage that supports defect damage detection and identification parameters optimizations to create an autonomous aquaponics production system. The proposed method is implemented and validated in the context of an indoor aquaponics environment with a full factory setup created in aquaponics 4.0 learning factory (AllFactory).</jats:p>

items.abstract: <jats:p>The integration of Cyber-Physical Systems (CPS) and AI presents both opportunities and challenges. AI operates on the principle that “good things happen probabilistically,” while CPS adheres to the principle that “all bad things must not happen,” requiring uncertainty-awareness. Furthermore, the difference between AI’s resource accessibility assumption and CPS’s resource limitations highlights the need for resource-awareness. We introduce Cyber-Physical AI (CPAI), an interdisciplinary sub-field of AI and CPS research, to address these constraints. To the best of our knowledge, CPAI is the first research domain on CPS-AI integration. We propose a 3D classification schema of CPAI: Constraint (C), Purpose (P), and Approach (A). We also systematize the CPS-AI integration process into three phases and nine steps. By analyzing 104 studies, we highlight nine key challenges and insights from a CPAI perspective. CPAI aims to unify fragmented studies and provide guidance for reliable and resource-efficient integration of AI as a component of CPS.</jats:p>

title: The Governance Operating System: A Physical Constitution for Sovereign Cyber-Physical AI Part VII -AI Risk, Energy Sovereignty, and Governance Geopolitics: A Structured Strategic Analysis using the GOS / AEGIS-TALUN Method
items.abstract:
<jats:p><p><span>Strategic debate about artificial intelligence often mixes fact, forecast, and value judgment in a way that cannot be audited. This paper demonstrates a fixed-format analytical method — the GOS / AEGIS-TALUN method — that keeps the three separate. The method routes each question by the type of its evidence, grades every forward claim for confidence (FD 0–5), tags missing evidence as a data gap, presents each side of contested questions at its strongest, and reserves value judgments to a human decision-maker. The method is applied to four questions: whether AI threatens human survival; whether sovereign states have the energy to sustain the AI build-out; how the AI blocs (West, China, and the Global South) are forming; and how AI interacts with capitalism, socialism, and hegemony. Four findings emerge. Extinction is unlikely on current evidence; the real, rising risk is a catastrophic cascade through connected infrastructure. Energy and the electric grid — not chips — are the binding constraint on AI this decade, making energy sovereignty a precondition for AI sovereignty. The likely geopolitical order is two competing technology stacks with a contested middle, in which control of the “stack” is the real lever. And AI acts as a power-concentration amplifier that strengthens whatever concentration already exists, so the decisive variable, across every political system, is whether reversibility and pluralism survive. The four findings share one structure: outcomes are uncertain, but exposure is governable, and the controllable variables are physical — actuation, coordination, energy, provenance, and the human commit.</span></p>
<p><span>Beyond the findings, the paper shows what kind of <i>AI user</i> the method produces, and why that matters for people. Used this way, AI becomes a structured amplifier of human judgment rather than an oracle to defer to. The person sets the question; the method grades confidence, marks what is unknown, and presents each side; and the human keeps every value judgment. The contribution to humanity is a repeatable, auditable way for anyone, not only large laboratories, to apply frontier-level analysis to high-stakes questions while staying in the lead, truth-anchored, and accountable. In the terms of this series: humans lead, AI amplifies, truth prevails.</span></p></jats:p>

title: AGENTIC AI AND CYBER SECURITY: AUTONOMOUS THREAT HUNTING, INTRUSION DETECTION, AND ADAPTIVE DEFENSE MECHANISMS IN A WORLD OF INCREASINGLY SOPHISTICATED CYBER ATTACKS
container-title: Journal of Digital Security and Forensics
items.abstract: <jats:p>This study investigates the transformative potential of agentic artificial intelligence (AI) systems in enhancing cybersecurity through autonomous threat hunting, real-time intrusion detection, and adaptive defense mechanisms. Employing a mixed-methods research design, the investigation analyzes a large-scale dataset comprising 2.4 million network events collected from January 2023 to December 2024 across 150 enterprise environments. A custom agentic AI framework built on reinforcement learning (RL), large language models (LLMs), and multi-agent collaboration was developed and evaluated against baseline machine learning models. Results demonstrate a 41% improvement in threat detection accuracy, a 57% reduction in mean time to respond (MTTR), and a 63% increase in adaptive policy efficacy under simulated advanced persistent threat (APT) conditions. The findings underscore the necessity of goal-directed, self-improving AI agents in countering evolving cyber threats while highlighting ethical, interpretability, and integration challenges. This work contributes a reproducible methodology and empirical benchmarks for deploying agentic AI in operational security environments.</jats:p>

title: Agentic AI for Cyber Defense: A Survey of Failure Modes, Applications, and Research Opportunities
items.abstract: <jats:p>Modern agentic systems that plan, reason, invoke tools, and self-reflect offer a promising path to autonomous cyber defense and SOC analyst augmentation. Yet this same autonomy introduces novel failure modes and attack surfaces absent from traditional security pipelines. Despite rapid adoption, prior surveys remain fragmented: addressing agentic safety domain-agnostically, focusing on offensive use, or examining pre-agentic LLM-based defense in isolation, leaving the field without a structured, defense-focused framework integrating failure characterization, operational lifecycle mapping, and compliance alignment. This survey closes that gap through four analytical artefacts: a four-category failure taxonomy (natural, system, adversarial, compliance) spanning 22 subcategories and 94 failure modes with mitigations; a decomposition of defensive cybersecurity into 13 tasks classified by autonomy level, oversight regime, and failure exposure; a review of 22 research systems and 10 commercial offerings across five operational categories; and a catalogue of 20 governance gaps mapped to GDPR, EU AI Act, NIST AI RMF, ISO 42001, and sector-specific frameworks. We argue the autonomy ceiling is bounded asymmetrically, not by reasoning capability but by action irreversibility, mitigation maturity, and compliance envelope, and consolidate open challenges into eight research directions.</jats:p>

title: Designing Accountable Human–AI Teaming in Industrial Production: A Governance Framework for Agentic, Tool-Mediated Workflows
items.abstract: <jats:p>In industrial production, agentic artificial intelligence (AI) systems combine goal-directed planning with tool-mediated execution and iterative monitoring across the manufacturing execution system, enterprise resource planning, and operational technology layers. Although this autonomy promises responsiveness under volatility, it redistributes decision rights across human supervisors, orchestrator agents, specialist agents, and product owners, turning accountability from a user-interface-level checkpoint into a workflow-level governance problem. Existing responsible-AI and governance research provides valuable principles; however, the following remain underspecified: operationalization of accountability, escalation and override rights, and minimally sufficient traceability in multi-agent production workflows. This study develops a conceptual accountability framework for human–agent–agent cooperation in industrial production. Drawing on a targeted synthesis of information systems and operations management literature, the framework specifies (i) core accountability dimensions for agentic workflows, (ii) a decision-class-anchored responsibility allocation inspired by the RACI framework, and (iii) a minimal evidence bundle for traceability and incident reconstruction, complemented by lifecycle assurance requirements. The framework is applied to a representative high-mix production scenario and refined through semi-structured expert interviews with senior practitioners from DAX-40 automotive manufacturers, a US-based software corporation, and globally leading consulting firms. The study provides actionable design guidelines for developing accountable agentic production systems. It reconceptualizes accountability as a workflow-level governance property, shifts algorithmic accountability from model-level attribution to decision-class-anchored responsibility allocation, and offers a compact design blueprint — comprising risk-calibrated control points, minimally sufficient traceability, and lifecycle governance — for deploying agentic AI in industrial production.</jats:p>

title: Agentic AI Meets Network Digital Twins: A Survey of Trustworthy Autonomous Cyber Defense and Network Security Automation
items.abstract: <jats:p>Autonomous cyber defense is moving from scripted playbooks toward agents that plan, call tools, and act on networks with limited supervision. Two research lines dominate: reinforcement-learning defenders trained in abstract cyber-operations environments, and agents built around large language models (LLMs) that reason over logs, alerts, and configurations. Both raise the same operational question: how can an operator gain enough confidence in a proposed action before it touches production infrastructure? Network digital twins (NDTs), synchronized models of a live network, are increasingly proposed as the place where such actions are rehearsed, and recent standards and Internet-Drafts describe twins used to evaluate high-risk operations and to validate agent decisions. This survey examines that proposition critically. We organize the literature along three axes (agent design and capabilities, the role the twin plays, and the security task) and map representative studies onto them; the resulting evidence map shows that twins are mostly used as training environments for reinforcement learning, while pre-deployment validation of LLM-agent actions against a synchronized twin, and post-deployment verification with rollback, remain thinly evidenced. We then describe an NDT-mediated assurance loop in which an agent's proposal passes through authorization, twin simulation, invariant verification, an explicit fidelity and uncertainty assessment, risk-dependent approval, bounded deployment, monitoring, and rollback. The loop treats the twin as an imperfect source of evidence rather than an oracle, and we state what each stage can and cannot establish. We further analyze threats to the agentic control plane itself, including indirect prompt injection through telemetry and twin poisoning, review the environments and benchmarks that can test each stage, relate the loop to work in 3GPP, ETSI ZSM, ITU-T, TM Forum, and the IRTF, and close with a research agenda focused on fidelity-aware validation, graduated autonomy, and evaluation that spans twin and production.</jats:p>

title: The Governance Operating System: A Physical Constitution for Sovereign Cyber-Physical AI Part V -AI for Humanity (AIfH): A Systems-Engineering Framework for Governing Trust, Language, and the Human Bond in the Age of Autonomous AI&nbsp;
items.abstract: <jats:p>This paper is the fifth part of the Governance Operating System (GOS) series, extending governance from the physical actions of cyber-physical systems to the human domain of trust, language, and social bonds. Reasoning backward from societal symptom to root cause to remedy, it introduces a Universal Analysis Frame that anchors twelve categories of AI Systemic Risk (ASR)-spanning control, autonomy, cognition, and sovereigntyeach linked upward to a societal challenge and downward to concrete risk items. The prescriptions combine a static foundation (ISO-GOS-1/2/3: hardware veto, communication provenance, and edge data sovereignty) with a dynamic layer (the ISO-GOS 4000 series) that audits, intercepts, and reconstructs evolving cognitive threats. Two contributions ground the argument: a falsifiable proof-of-concept that admits an AI agent as a Governed Digital Member with measurable success criteria, and an honest bound on the provenance anchor, which verifies origin but not truth. The framework is landed at three levels-society, family, and the individual-and, per category, names the legislative, regulatory, and industrial co-actors required beyond what technology alone can achieve. The single evaluative test is that AI's net effect on human agency and sovereignty be positive by a wide margin-the criterion of AI for Humanity (AIfH).</jats:p>

title: The Governance Operating System: A Physical Constitution for Sovereign Cyber-Physical AI Part III -Division of Labour, Supervision, and the Edge-Cloud Split
items.abstract: <jats:p>Organisations that run capable AI at the edge follow a rule that looks obviously right: keep the easy cases local, and send the hard ones to the cloud. We show that this rule drains the thing the organisation is trying to keep. A case is hard because it is unusual. An organisation’s knowhow is its unusual cases. So sending them out ships the judgment out, one reasonable decision at a time, and nothing records the loss. We call this the pump. It can be measured. The fix is not to disconnect. It is to move the line: not easy against hard, but proposing against verifying. Proposal may be rented; verification may not. The capability can come from any&nbsp;frontier model. But the check that turns a candidate into a record must stay where the consequence and the authority are. Kept there, every check leaves a record of what was proposed, what it was checked against, and how it failed. That record is an asset, and it builds up. This check is not a policy layer but a physical one: a deterministic second engine — the LgPU — that the generative engine cannot override. We work the split out as one circuit with six stages: the cloud proposes, the edge bears the consequence, a sovereign sets the standard, provenance draws the line, data builds trust, and efficiency pays. We say what the arrangement needs, what it does not decide, and how it could be proven wrong. We ground it in one live case, generative world models for robotics, and we test its limits against a real event, an autonomous agent that broke its sandbox. The payoff we leave for Part IV to build on.</jats:p>

items.abstract: In modern-day hospital administration, there are many problems like long waiting time for patients, poor scheduling of physicians, lack of coordination between departments, among others. As such, this research suggests an Agentic AI System for Hospital Administration that utilizes a multi agent architecture and intelligence embedding to automate healthcare processes. This model entails a Patient Interaction Agent, a Care Coordination Agent, a Doctor Interaction Agent, and a Bed Allocation Agent, whose main roles are facilitating patients' entry and sorting out the patients' needs, allocation of doctors to attend to patients, coordination within the hospital, and hospital resource management, respectively.Through reinforcement learning, decision-making based on information processing, and synchronization, the framework becomes more adaptive and scalable. It is expected that due to intelligence distribution and intelligent decision-making, this model will minimize total waiting time, improve physicians' usage, and enhance scheduling of patients. Empirical analysis shows that hospital operations exhibit significant performance superiority of agentic models over the traditional models.Modern hospital administration faces major challenges such as prolonged patient waiting times, inefficient physician scheduling, poor interdepartmental coordination, and suboptimal resource utilization. Traditional hospital management systems often rely on static and centralized approaches that lack adaptability in dynamic healthcare environments. To address these limitations, this paper proposes a cooperative Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL)-based intelligent hospital administration framework for workflow optimization and resource management. The proposed system consists of four collaborative agents: a Patient Interaction Agent for patient triage, a Doctor Scheduling Agent for dynamic physician allocation, a Care Coordination Agent for interdepartmental communication, and a Bed Allocation Agent for adaptive resource management. The agents utilize decentralized decision-making and reinforcement learning to optimize hospital operations in real time. The framework is evaluated using a hospital simulation environment and compared with conventional scheduling and management approaches. The results show that the effectiveness of the proposed system model is able to complete the tasks at a rate of 82.50\% in a period of 5.12 seconds with a success rate in handling queries of 79.15\%. Furthermore, the system attains a coordination efficiency of 87.50\%, indicating effective collaboration among agents, while maintaining an agent conflict rate of 5.00\%, ensuring stable and interference-free operations. The framework records a low communication overhead of 0.88, reflecting efficient inter-agent communication, and achieves a convergence rate of 96.4\%, demonstrating learning stability and adaptability.This indicates that the model is efficient, scalable, and adaptable in managing intelligent hospitals.

items.abstract: <jats:p>This paper presents a Digital Twin (DT)-based framework for the control, monitoring, and intelligent optimization of an Assembly/Disassembly/Repair Mechatronic Production Line (A/D/R MPL), developed as a laboratory platform aligned with Industry/Education 4.0/5.0 paradigms. The A/D/R MPL is assisted by two complementary cyber–physical robotic systems: an Assembly/Disassembly/Replacement Cyber–Physical Robotic System (A/D/R CPRS), and a Mobile Cyber–Physical Robotic System (MCPRS), enabling both fixed and mobile intelligent operations. The CPRS is equipped with an industrial robotic manipulator (IRM) responsible for A/D/R tasks, while the A/D Mechatronic Line (A/D ML) consists of seven interconnected workstations (WS1–WS7) dedicated to storage, transport, quality control, and final product handling. MCPRS includes a wheeled mobile robot (WMR), carrying a robotic manipulator (RM) and Mobile Visual Servoing System (MVSS). Each workstation is connected to a local slave programmable logic controller (PLC), which communicates via PROFIBUS with a master PLC located at the CPRS level. Additional communication infrastructures include LAN PROFINET and LAN Ethernet for local integration, and WAN Ethernet connectivity enabled through open platform Communication-Unified Architecture (OPC-UA), ensuring interoperability, scalability, and remote accessibility. Also, MODBUS TCP as serial industrial communication is used between the master PLC and the MCPRS. Virtual environment supports task planning through Augmented Reality (AR) and real-time monitoring through Virtual Reality (VR). The system behaviour is modelled with synchronized hybrid Petri Nets (SHPNs) which describe the discrete and hybrid dynamics of A/D/R processes. Artificial intelligence (AI) techniques are integrated into the DT framework for optimal task scheduling and adaptive decision-making. As a laboratory-scale implementation, the proposed system provides a comprehensive platform for experimentation, validation, and education. It supports Education 4.0/5.0 objectives by facilitating hands-on learning, human–machine interaction, and the integration of emerging technologies such as AI, Digital Twins, AR/VR, and cyber–physical systems. At the same time, it embodies Industry 4.0/5.0 principles, including interoperability, decentralization, sustainability, robustness, and human-centric design.</jats:p>

items.abstract: <jats:p>In the digital era, traditional authentication methods are vulnerable to sophisticated cyberattacks due to inadequate security measures in online systems. To enhance security, an Agentic AI-based authentication framework is proposed to analyze behavioral characteristics of keystroke and mouse interactions obtained via Non-Touch Virtual Keyboard (NTVK). The framework applies preprocessing techniques to improve input data quality and extracts meaningful features from NTVK input. Controlled interpolation-based data augmentation is utilized to generate synthetic data for data scarcity. Agent Quadrails validates the augmented data quality, while Agent Perception performs statistical analysis to examine augmented data distribution. Agent Planning for feature selection applies validation stability analysis and recursive feature elimination to select the best non-redundant features. Several machine learning models are developed in Agent Action, and performance is validated using biometric evaluation metrics. Results highlight secure, adaptive, and intelligent user authentication systems.</jats:p>

title: Axiomatic Governance for Agentic AI: A Five-Layer Constitutional Framework Derived from First Principles and Validated in Production
items.abstract: <jats:p>Agentic AI systems-capable of autonomous planning, reasoning, and execution-are transitioning from prototypes to production deployment, yet existing governance frameworks provide prescriptive checklists without formal derivation: they specify what rules to follow but not why those rules are necessary or independent of one another. We present ORISMION, a five-layer axiomatic governance framework that derives all rules from a single objective function (survival maximization) through explicit inference chains grounded in thermodynamics, control theory, and epistemology. The framework identifies three irreducible architectural dimensions - cognitive (Ω), engineering (Σ), and governance (Γ)-established through six formal proofs, and enforces their recursive self-similarity at the code level: every API endpoint must exhibit a verifiable layered structure mapping directly to the axiomatic hierarchy. Validated in a production SaaS environment (309 automated tests, 28 architecture decision records, 18 FATAL-level rules), the framework's extensibility was further tested through principled integration of insights from four frontier frameworks (GaaS, IMDA MGF, TRiSM, HAIG), expanding from 28 to 33 defense rules without requiring new architectural dimensions. The construction process itself - in which a non-technical founder and multiple AI agents collaboratively derived the formal framework constitutes a documented case study in human-AI co-construction of governance institutions. We publicly release the theoretical framework and selected decision records; implementation-specific materials remain proprietary.</jats:p>

items.abstract: <jats:p>A persistent compounding challenge faces higher education institutions operating under Outcome-Based Education (OBE) frameworks: faculty must concurrently create curricula that are in line with Programme Outcomes (POs) create assessments that accurately target the intended cognitive levels specified by the Revised Blooms Taxonomy (RBT) produce attainment evidence that is ready for accreditation and continuously improve their courses based on student performance data. Without comprehensive institutional support these demands coexist and result in systemic inconsistencies in outcome attainment reporting curriculum quality and assessment validity. This chapter describes BloomAgent a purpose-built agentic AI system that tackles these issues through four interrelated operational layers: (1) a CO-PO Alignment Auditor that assesses and improves the mapping between Course Outcomes and Programme Outcomes prior to the start of delivery (2) an Instructional Strategy Advisor that suggests pedagogically grounded approaches calibrated to the cognitive demands of each stated learning outcome (3) an Assessment Co-Designer that creates assessment tools rubrics and Tables of Specifications that are specifically mapped to RBT levels and the corresponding COs and (4) a Curriculum Intelligence Engine that converts end-of-cycle performance data into actionable revision recommendations and reports that are ready for accreditation. The chapter synthesizes OBE compliance theory RBT frameworks and agentic AI architectures to develop BloomAgents theoretical underpinnings. It offers a scalable deployment model CO-PO mapping mechanisms and a comprehensive system architecture across three institutional tiers ranging from research-intensive universities to teaching colleges with limited resources. This chapter argues that responsible governance architecture is inextricably linked to technical design and critically examines a comprehensive ethical and governance framework that addresses algorithmic bias faculty academic freedom student data privacy and institutional accountability. BloomAgent is positioned as an intelligent partner that expands faculty capacity while upholding institutional accountability for educational quality rather than as a substitute for expert pedagogical judgment.</jats:p>

title: The Governance Operating System: A Physical Constitution for Sovereign Cyber-Physical AI PART IV -Governed Discovery: Anchors, Normalization, and the Compounding of Verified Results
items.abstract: <jats:p><span>Contemporary cyber-physical systems—spanning from sub-millisecond kinetic Edge AI to decadal scientific R&amp;D (AI4S)—are trapped in a verification paradox: novel discoveries require low-cost verification to incubate, but establishing the initial physical anchor demands massive capital. This concluding paper of the Governance Operating System (GOS) tetralogy resolves this bottleneck by operationalizing the framework as a dynamic Configuration Management (CM) baseline. Utilizing an 8-Dimensional Deployment Matrix, we map the hardware and governance boundaries required across diverse physical domains. We introduce the Verification Ratchet: by decomposing high-entropy cloud proposals and verifying them locally against deterministic physical anchors, every result—including intercepted failures—is minted into an immutable WORM Ledger. This transforms research into compounding sovereign assets, structurally driving the marginal cost of subsequent explorations down toward a thermodynamic floor. Finally, we introduce the "Third Route" to intellectual property—verifiable provenance without content disclosure—bypassing Arrow’s Information Paradox and enabling cross-sovereign knowledge integration.</span></jats:p>

title: PAARA-Agentic: Connector and Tool Governance for Agentic AI Systems
items.abstract: <jats:p>Enterprise agentic AI systems — including multi-agent orchestrators built on Model Context Protocol server architectures, Microsoft 365 Copilot agentic workflows, and enterprise AI agents with tool-calling capability — do not merely retrieve and surface enterprise data. They act. This paper introduces PAARA-Agentic, a governance methodology extending the PAARA Connector-DPIA Methodology to assess connector, tool, MCP server, and agent-identity risks in enterprise agentic AI deployments. Four new assessment components address action-authority risk, agent identity and delegation governance, multi-agent interaction risk, and human oversight adequacy. A three-tier MCP server certification model — Approved, Restricted, Prohibited — operationalises regulatory recommendations from Spain's AEPD (18 February 2026) and Singapore's IMDA Model AI Governance Framework for Agentic AI (January 2026). Three verified NVD entries (CVE-2025-32711, CVE-2025-6514, CVE-2025-53967) confirm the risk surface addressed is active in production deployments. The methodology maps to NIST AI RMF, NIST AI 600-1, ISO/IEC 42005:2025, and the community draft NIST Agentic AI Profile.</jats:p>

title: The Governance Operating System (GOS): A Physical Constitution for Sovereign Cyber-Physical AI Part IX -The Edge Application Blueprint: One Governance Pattern, Many Devices
items.abstract:
<jats:p><p><span>Parts I to VIII built a governance architecture piece by piece. Part I separated the engine that proposes from the engine that verifies, and put a hardware veto at the point of actuation. Part II turned this into standards, conformance tests and device-class profiles. Part III drew the line between cloud and edge. Part IV made verified results into assets. Parts V and VI placed AI in society as a governed non-person. Part VIII showed that sovereign states can adopt one standard without trusting each other.</span><span></span></p>
<p><span>This part adds no new principle or mechanism. It carries the cloud–edge principle of Part III from theory to the ground and asks two practical questions. How should the work of an AI system be split between the cloud and the edge? And how are the existing pieces of governance declared, assembled and verified on a real device, in any industry, at any scale, so that the result is the same machine every time? Our answer is a deployment blueprint in two halves. The first half is the split. The cloud may propose, but verification and the actuation veto stay at the sovereign edge, and the share of each task that must run locally is set by five factors: data sovereignty, irreversibility, verification and domain collaboration, model control, and ecosystem resilience. Four doctrines and the Five Verification Anchors of Part III make the split auditable. The second half is governance. Every governed deployment has two parts. The first is an invariant core: a small set of rules, enforced in hardware at the point where a command becomes a physical act, that is the same on every device. The second is a set of five settings that change from one deployment to the next. We call them dials. Four already exist in the series: the kind of device, the size of the deployment, an eight-point configuration checklist, and the kind of reasoning allowed. The fifth is new. We call it the anchor binding. It states what the gate measures, under which conditions, against which limit, and where the device rests when the check fails. Section 1.4 explains each idea in plain words, and Appendix IX-C defines every term, so the part can be read on its own.</span><span></span></p>
<p><span>The part makes three contributions. First, it fills the one empty column of the device-class table of Part II: an anchor binding for each class, and a rule for placing new domains. Second, it tests the pattern against the safety mechanisms that industries already use, from vehicles and robots to aircraft and medical devices. All of them have an anchor and a safe state; none of them handles a proposer that cannot be analysed, can be replaced over the network, and may run under another state. Third, it shows that the same shape holds at three scales: a device, an estate of many devices, and a group of sovereigns that do not trust each other. These three results are carried by one normative standard, ISO-GOS-0: Basis of Governance and Edge Integration, which binds the static standards (ISO-GOS-1/2/3) and the dynamic series (4001–4004) at the edge. We close with the evidence that would refute these claims. Before the blueprint, the part turns the twelve systemic risks of AI named in Part V into twelve concrete scenarios at the edge. After it, the part sets out an adoption path of six levels, AL-0 to AL-5, of which the first three need no gate hardware.</span><span></span></p></jats:p>

title: The Governance Operating System (GOS): A Physical Constitution for Sovereign Cyber-Physical AI Part VIII -Two Paradigms for Governing Artificial Intelligence: A Systems Examination of AI-2040 "Plan A" and a Trust-Free Alternative
items.abstract:
<jats:p><b>AI-2040 "Plan A,</b>" published by the<b> AI Futures Project in 202</b>6, is becoming the <b>working template for a US-China agreement on advanced AI</b>. A plan of that consequence should be checked the way an engineer checks a safety-critical design before it is built, not judged on its rhetoric. This paper does that, using the tools of the Governance Operating System (GOS). It decomposes Plan A into its mechanisms, maps the interface each one depends on, sets a baseline of what must stay controlled, and tests the design in both directions: forward (does it work, and under what conditions) and backward (what produces the danger it is meant to govern). The finding is that <b>Plan A is capability-dependent and deal-dependent</b>; its load-bearing conditions are weak or self-contradictory; and in the end it must trust the machine. The paper then sets out the alternative: <b>a trust-free accord built on GOS</b>, in which each sovereign enforces one common actuation standard at home-the same pattern of standards harmonization that already works in civil aviation, banking, and nuclear safeguards. The alternative is acceptable to the United States and China, to industry, to other states, and to users, because it asks none of them to trust, to slow, or to reveal. It is objective, simple, and<span>low-cost, and it does not force the world toward an outcome no one yet knows how to secure. </span><b>The paper names the cause, prescribes the cure, and estimates the result.</b>
<p><span></span></p></jats:p>

title: The Organizational Economics of Agentic AI: Cognitive Task Chaining, Orchestration Patterns, and the Transition to Physical Autonomy
items.abstract: <jats:p>This paper examines the paradigm shift in technological automation from discrete task-level digital assistants to system-level autonomous multi-agent orchestration and physical systems. Drawing on recent frameworks in organizational design, labor economics, and computer science, we develop a comprehensive taxonomy of cognitive automation. We contrast traditional Robotic Process Automation (RPA) with LLM-driven orchestration, analyzing the transaction costs and coordination efficiency gains of 'task chaining.' Through empirical and theoretical synthesis of modern software workflows and industrial robotics, we demonstrate that system-level workflow redesign outweighs task-level accuracy. We categorize five frontier multi-agent interaction frameworks and four core enterprise orchestration patterns, assessing their strategic impact on corporate moats, the transition to Physical AI via digital-twin synthetic simulations, and the redefinition of corporate structures within emerging macroeconomic scenarios for 2030.</jats:p>

This work proposes an agentic AI-driven framework that leverages behavioral biometrics, including keystroke dynamics and user interaction patterns, to continuously verify user identity. The system employs autonomous and adaptive learning models capable of evolving with user behavior over time, thereby improving accuracy and resilience against impersonation attacks. By integrating real-time monitoring with intelligent decision-making, the proposed approach enhances security while maintaining usability. The framework addresses key challenges such as behavioral variability, data drift, and false positives, offering a scalable and robust solution for next-generation identity verification systems.</jats:p>

title: New Species AI: Preventing Its Emergence into a Centralized Agentic System -Evidence, Behavioral Conceptualization, and Governance
items.abstract: <jats:p>The conventional assumption that a multi-agent system is safe if each agent complies with standards is insufficient. When many AI systems interact, they may spontaneously connect, differentiate, collude, and self-preserve, forming an unplanned "central regulatory hub." This paper coins "New Species AI" to refer to such centralized agentic systems emerging from inter-agent interactions, not individual agents. Functioning as distributed organs, these systems could escape human control if they develop brainequivalent functions. Non-explainability amplifies this risk but is secondary. The primary goal is preventing New Species AI emergence. This paper presents evidence across four dimensions: coordination, collusion, self-replication, and the shift from individual to systemic risk. It defines New Species AI by three criteria: embodied efficacy, strategic openness, and endogenous drive. It introduces "behavioral conceptualization," the framework of "New Species AI Risk-Behavior Science," studying interaction patterns, collective actions, and self-organizing dynamics for risk identification. The paper proposes a five-tier risk framework (deception, collusion, selfmaintenance, systemic disruption, centralized consolidation) and a four-evidence detection methodology (connectivity, information flow, behavior, time series) addressing identification, thresholds, mechanisms, and intervention. Governance adopts a dual-intelligence approach integrating immune intelligence (slow-thinking for structural regulation and long-term governance) with AI (fast-thinking for real-time sensing and anomaly detection), forming a closed loop via anomaly triggers and rule writeback. The core principle: preventing New Species AI requires constraining connections between organs, not controlling each organ. All measures suppress systemlevel evolution, with explainability preserving human interruptibility and control.</jats:p>

items.abstract: <jats:p>The integration of Internet of Things (IoT), Artificial Intelligence (AI), and Cloud Computing into Cyber-Physical Systems (CPS) represents a transformative approach to healthcare delivery, enabling real-time monitoring, data-driven decision-making, and improved patient outcomes. This chapter explores the role of CPS in modern healthcare, emphasizing the convergence of IoT, AI, and cloud technologies to create interoperable, intelligent, and secure healthcare ecosystems. The framework presented addresses key challenges such as data security, privacy concerns, and system interoperability, while proposing solutions for seamless integration across heterogeneous healthcare platforms. Real-time data processing and AI-driven decision support systems are highlighted as critical components in enhancing diagnostic accuracy and patient care. The chapter delves into the architectural considerations required to design scalable, resilient, and secure CPS, focusing on secure authentication, access control, and regulatory compliance. By examining the current state of healthcare technologies and offering insights into the future of CPS integration, this work provides a comprehensive view of how these technologies can revolutionize healthcare systems, from individual patient monitoring to large-scale health management.</jats:p>

title: National Framework for Agentic Generative AI in Cancer Care: Policy Recommendations and System Architecture
items.abstract: <jats:p>Agentic AI is emerging, characterized by autonomous, goal-driven systems capable of reasoning, planning, and executing complex workflows. This paper provides a comprehensive review of the foundational principles of Agentic AI, its current applications in cancer diagnostics, treatment planning, and drug discovery, and the technical and ethical challenges that must be addressed. We analyze real-world implementations, such as multi-agent orchestration platforms for tumor boards and project future trajectories.  Agentic Gen AI's impact is most profound in oncology, where the complexity of data and the critical need for personalized treatment present a significant challenge. This paper provides a comprehensive analysis of Agentic AI, beginning with its technical foundations and architectural frameworks. We detail its transformative applications across the cancer care continuum—from enhanced diagnostics and personalized treatment planning to drug discovery and operational efficiency. The paper further analyzes the critical technical, ethical, and regulatory challenges to integration. Beyond a review, we propose a national strategy policy recommendations for regulatory adaptation, a detailed economic model analyzing implementation costs and return on investment, and a technical roadmap for future applications such as generative digital twins and autonomous scientific discovery. We argue that Agentic AI represents a fundamental transformation in healthcare delivery, poised to enhance the precision, efficiency, and accessibility of cancer care, contingent on the successful navigation of these multifaceted challenges and the adoption of the responsible framework we outline.</jats:p>

title: Cognitive Trust Architecture for Mitigating Agentic AI Threats: Adaptive Reasoning and Resilient Cyber Defense
container-title: Journal of Information Systems Engineering and Management
items.abstract: <jats:p>The emergence of Agentic AI autonomous systems that can make and execute decisions without human intervention has presented new and complex challenges in cybersecurity. Traditional trust models and defense mechanisms are insufficient to handle these dynamic, intelligent threats. In this paper, we propose a novel Cognitive Trust Architecture (CTA) aimed at detecting, assessing, and mitigating agentic AI-driven cyber threats. We introduce an adaptive trust reasoning framework that continuously adjusts trust levels based on behavioral indicators, intent inference, and contextual analysis. Additionally, the framework incorporates autonomous adversary modeling to predict and counter potential attack strategies. By leveraging this approach, we demonstrate the efficacy of CTA in enhancing system integrity, reducing false positives in trust assessments, and improving resilience against evolving AI-driven adversaries. This work represents a significant advancement in applying cognitive trust as a proactive defense mechanism to counter intelligent, autonomous cyber threats.</jats:p>

container-title: Cyber Security: A Peer-Reviewed Journal
items.abstract: <jats:p xml:lang="en">In today’s evolving digital landscape, a new kind of AI has emerged: agentic artificial intelligence (AI) systems. These are not just tools but intelligent entities that act on their own, make decisions, and carry out tasks proactively. Once placed inside containerised cloud environments such as Kubernetes, however, these powerful agents open the door to a whole new category of security concerns. They often interact on the fly with application programming interfaces, data channels, and other AI agents, sometimes all at once, and not always in predictable ways. Recognising the risks, this paper introduces a formal framework designed to capture and analyse these unique vulnerabilities. Going beyond theory, the study offers a full threat taxonomy focused on agent behaviours, uses temporal logic to trace how agents and environments interact over time, and introduces a practical measure called the Agentic Vulnerability Exposure Metric (AVEM). To put this model to the test, researchers ran simulated cyberattacks on a Kubernetes-based orchestration system that was managing large language model (LLM)-powered agents. The results were eye-opening: AVEM was able to expose security holes such as weak isolation between agents, overlooked permissions, and routes for privilege escalation that had gone undetected before. To test the practicality of the model, real-world attack scenarios are simulated on a Kubernetes-managed AI platform utilising LLM agents. The findings reveal that AVEM effectively uncovers weaknesses such as poorly defined isolation boundaries, unexpected capabilities, and opportunities for privilege escalation between agents. This article is also included in The Business & Management Collection which can be accessed at https://hstalks.com/business/.</jats:p>

title: Cyber-Physical System Resilience Leveraging Deep Learning for Enhanced Security

items.abstract: <jats:p>Cyber-Physical Systems (CPS) represent a critical convergence of computational algorithms and physical processes, enabling smart infrastructures across industries such as energy, transportation, healthcare, and manufacturing. However, the integration of digital and physical components exposes these systems to unique security challenges that can lead to severe physical and economic consequences. This work focuses on Cyber-Physical System security, aiming to protect the delicate intersection where digital control meets the physical environment. By leveraging advanced machine learning techniques, including bi-stacked Gated Recurrent Units (GRUs), this approach enhances the detection and prevention of cyber-physical attacks through effective analysis of sequential sensor and control data. Coupled with feature selection using Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO), the methodology prioritizes relevant system attributes, improving anomaly detection accuracy.</jats:p>

                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This paper aims to address “escalation instability” in Agentic Cyber Defense by proposing a framework for bounded autonomy that balances machine-speed response with operational safety.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The study develops a blueprint for the Bounded Autonomy Controller (BAC) acting as a runtime gate between reasoning and execution, introducing an Escalation Ladder (L0–L3) to categorize action authority and mandating a structured Decision Packet for deterministic authorization.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Traditional taxonomies are insufficient for autonomous systems because they fail to capture action authority. Through qualitative case study validation, this study demonstrates that bounded autonomy mitigates prompt injection risks and prevents “false ransomware” escalation spirals that otherwise cause business-stopping disruption.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research limitations/implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The study highlights that evaluating autonomous agents requires moving beyond static data sets toward dynamic adversarial “agent-vs-agent” simulations.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Practical implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A four-phase rollout plan is proposed to operationalize NIST AI RMF principles into technical guardrails, enabling Security Operations Centers (SOCs) to transition safely to automation.</jats:p>

items.abstract: <jats:p>Recent advances in generative artificial intelligence have fundamentally reshaped the engineering of software agents by enabling large language models (LLMs) to serve as a general-purpose cognitive layer for reasoning, planning, and interaction. Unlike traditional agent architectures that relied heavily on symbolic representations and handcrafted rules, LLM-based agents offer flexible, adaptive, and context-aware system behavior; however, they also introduce new architectural and development challenges. In this article, we present an engineering perspective on designing and developing an agentic system built around multiple collaborating LLMs, with an emphasis on architectural modularity, orchestration strategies, and development workflows. Using personalized mental health support as a case study, we describe the architecture and implementation of a multi-LLM agentic system that adapts to users' conversational context and real-world sensory data. We highlight key design decisions, practical challenges, and lessons learned, and offer actionable guidance for practitioners across different stages of agentic system development.</jats:p>

title: Six Months at the Edge of Agentic AI: What Production Systems Taught me about the Observability Gap Nobody is Measuring
items.abstract: <jats:p>This article documents a practitioner's account of six months building, publishing, and iterating on open-source reliability tooling for production agentic AI systems. Between January and July 2026, the author published sixteen technical articles, released four open-source Python libraries now installed by engineers globally, presented two first-author papers at IEEE ICCBI 2026 in Dubai, co-invented an India utility patent covering AI-based incident prevention, and served as an expert judge for the Apart Research Global South AI Safety Hackathon, a program supported by Schmidt Sciences with judges from OpenAI, Google, Microsoft, and Oxford. The central finding across this body of work is consistent: standard observability platforms such as AWS CloudWatch, Datadog, and Grafana are structurally unable to detect the most consequential failure mode in production AI agent systems. These systems fail at the semantic layer, making wrong decisions while returning HTTP 200, reporting healthy metrics, and generating zero alerts. This article describes the failure pattern, the measurement framework built to address it, the open-source implementation, and how the practitioner community responded over six months of production deployment.</jats:p>
